comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C8-C12, C37-C38. Both evaluations find the evidence for stochastic gravity representation (Gaussian distribution with σ=19.9°) to be well-supported. Reviewers explicitly affirm the finding that participants model gravity as a distribution rather than a fixed vector, describing the experimental evidence as 'generally solid.'

Perfect agreement on claims C13-C14, C39-C40. Both evaluations support the cognitive impenetrability findings. OpenEval emphasizes the high correlation and lack of significant difference in σ values, while peer reviewers acknowledge the control experiments address alternative explanations, with the editor noting these experiments 'address some of the most pressing concerns.'

Strong agreement on claims C15-C18 regarding MGS superiority over NGS. OpenEval focuses on the elimination of systematic bias, while peer review R3 also includes C19-C20 and emphasizes the model's ability to explain the height-dependent instability illusion. Both find the evidence solid and consistent.

Partial overlap on claims C19-C20. OpenEval R4 focuses specifically on the height-dependent instability illusion and its parsimonious explanation through MGS. Peer R3 groups this with the broader model comparison (C15-C18), treating it as part of the overall evidence that the stochastic model fits human behavior better.

Strong agreement on claims C21-C23, C61-C62 regarding reinforcement learning origins. OpenEval notes the close match between model σ=21.6 and human σ=19.9 but emphasizes this is computational plausibility rather than proof. Peer reviewers affirm this 'lends support' and 'suggests that this distribution is learned through experience,' treating it as strong supporting evidence.

Strong agreement on claims C24-C26 regarding ecological advantage. OpenEval notes the efficiency metric is somewhat arbitrary but the statistical comparisons are significant. Peer reviewers describe this as providing 'a normative explanation based on a resource-rational framework' that balances speed and accuracy.

Perfect agreement on claims C27-C28. Both evaluations support the finding that three simulations best match human variance patterns. OpenEval notes this involves inferential leaps about cognitive strategy. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this as part of the overall model validation without raising specific concerns.

Strong agreement on background claims C1-C7, C33-C34. OpenEval notes these appropriately cite prior literature but cannot fully verify without checking sources. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this background framing by not questioning it, focusing instead on novel findings. Peer R9 also includes C35-C36, C55-C57 which OpenEval addresses separately in R13.

Perfect agreement on methodological claims C41-C45. Both evaluations find the methods, sample sizes, exclusion criteria, and ethical approval appropriate and standard. OpenEval describes these as 'straightforward and appropriate,' while peer reviewers do not raise concerns and note methodological rigor was scrutinized.

Significant disagreement on claims C46-C47 regarding theoretical distinguishability. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, arguing the cognitive impenetrability findings support parsimony for the stochastic model, though noting the distinction may be about explanatory preference. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, stating 'The possibility of inferred external perturbations...is difficult to rule out' and 'it will likely take many, clever studies, to fully reconcile these two alternative accounts.'

Disagreement on evaluation type for claims C48-C50, C63-C67. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting these are 'largely speculative interpretations' involving theoretical proposals (predictive coding, active inference) and future applications not empirically tested. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the theoretical framework as 'reasonable extensions of the empirical findings' and noting the normative explanation based on resource-rational framework.

Strong agreement on main conclusion claims C29, C52-C54. OpenEval notes these appropriately synthesize key contributions without overstating conclusions. Peer reviewers explicitly support the main conclusions, describing this as 'a valuable study' with 'generally solid' evidence. Peer R8 also includes C30-C32 and C53 which OpenEval addresses in other results.

Agreement on claim C51 regarding significance as world model example. OpenEval groups this with other summary statements (C29, C52-C54) as appropriately synthesizing findings. Peer reviewers implicitly support this through overall positive assessment, describing it as 'a valuable study' presenting 'surprising findings.'

Agreement on theoretical framing claims C35-C36, C55-C57. OpenEval finds the distinction between external noise and internal stochastic representation conceptually clear and supported by cognitive impenetrability evidence. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this background framing as established context. Peer R9 also includes background claims C1-C7, C33-C34 which OpenEval addresses in R8.

Partial overlap on claims C58-C59 regarding theoretical distinction. OpenEval R13 treats these as part of the theoretical framing that is SUPPORTED by cognitive impenetrability evidence. Peer R7 addresses the broader theoretical distinguishability (C46-C47, C58-C59) and rates as UNCERTAIN, noting difficulty in fully ruling out alternative accounts.

Minor overlap on claim C30. OpenEval R4 focuses on the height-dependent instability illusion as evidence for MGS. Peer R8 includes C30 as part of the broader main conclusions, treating it as one component of the overall supported findings about stochastic world models.

Minor overlap on claim C32. OpenEval R6 addresses the ecological advantage and efficiency analysis. Peer R8 includes C32 as part of the main conclusions summary, treating it as one aspect of the overall supported account.

Minor overlap on claim C31. OpenEval R5 focuses on the computational modeling of learning origins. Peer R8 includes C31 as part of the main conclusions, treating it as one component of the overall evidence for stochastic representation.

Minor overlap on claim C60. OpenEval R5 includes C60 as part of the computational modeling evidence (rated SUPPORTED). Peer R11 includes C60 as part of theoretical interpretations and implications (rated SUPPORTED), treating it as a reasonable extension of empirical findings.
